intro: Nuclear medicine technologists handle radioactive materials safely and care for patients, skills shared with radiation therapy and nuclear technology. The closest of the 25 careers below is Radiation Therapists, with a 92% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $105,310, which is 4% more than the $101,370 nuclear medicine technologists earn.
why_it_works: Each scan means preparing doses precisely, operating imaging equipment and keeping patients calm and still. O*NET rates social perceptiveness at 3.38 out of 5 for this job, and judgment, coordination and service orientation at 3.25. Radiation therapy, nuclear monitoring and respiratory care use the same safety habits. Some matches need extra training. The gaps are complex problem solving and operations analysis.
tips: Radiation therapy is the closest move and often needs only a short additional program.
Nuclear Technicians earn $110,240, which is 9% more, outside health care.
Nuclear Power Reactor Operators earn $122,890, or 21% more, and value radiation safety training.

faq.q: What jobs can former nuclear medicine technologists do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Radiation Therapists (92%), nuclear monitoring technicians (78%) and Respiratory Therapists (75%), based on O*NET 31.0. Nuclear Technicians are 66% matched and earn $110,240, which is 9% more than the $101,370 nuclear medicine median.

faq.q: Which careers for nuclear medicine technologists pay more?
faq.a: 6 of the 25 matches pay more. Nurse Anesthetists earn $236,590 (133% more), Nuclear Power Reactor Operators $122,890 (21% more) and health and safety engineers $115,160 (14% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Nurse anesthesia needs a graduate degree.

faq.q: Do nuclear medicine technologists need more education to switch?
faq.a: Sometimes. 17 of the 25 matches need no more education than nuclear medicine technologists already have, including 6 of the top 10. An associate degree is common in the closest match, held by 50% of workers, though each field has its own certification.

faq.q: What skills should nuclear medicine technologists learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are complex problem solving, service orientation, operations analysis and operations monitoring. Coordination already rates 3.25 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so plant operations and safety analysis are the main steps outside hospitals.
